answer_text:
Define

\[
g(x)=e^{-x}f(x).
\]

Since \(f>0\), \(g\) is well-defined. Differentiating,

\[
g'(x)=e^{-x}f'(x)-e^{-x}f(x)=e^{-x}\bigl(f'(x)-f(x)\bigr)>0.
\]

So \(g\) is strictly increasing and positive. Pick some \(x_0\) and let \(c=g(x_0)>0\). Then for \(x>x_0\),

\[
g(x)>c,
\]

hence

\[
f(x)=e^xg(x)>c e^x.
\]

Now if \(k<1\), choose \(X>x_0\) large enough that

\[
c e^{(1-k)X}>1.
\]

Then for all \(x\ge X\),

\[
f(x)>c e^x=e^{kx}c e^{(1-k)x}>e^{kx}.
\]

Thus the inequality is guaranteed for every \(k<1\).

The endpoint \(k=1\) is not guaranteed in general. For example,

\[
f(x)=e^x\left(1-e^{-e^x}\right)
\]

satisfies \(f(x)>0\) and

\[
f'(x)-f(x)=e^{2x-e^x}>0,
\]

but

\[
\frac{f(x)}{e^x}=1-e^{-e^x}<1
\]

for all \(x\), so \(f(x)>e^x\) is false. Also, for \(k>1\),

\[
\frac{f(x)}{e^{kx}}\to 0.
\]

Therefore the hypothesis guarantees \(f(x)>e^{kx}\) for all sufficiently large \(x\) exactly for \(k<1\). The sharp threshold value is

\[
\boxed{1\text{ (with all }k<1\text{ guaranteed)}}.
\]
